title: The H1 Heading
summary: An H1 names the whole page. Browsers draw it large, but its real job is meaning — for readers, search engines, and screen readers.
objectives: Explain what an H1 is and why it exists
Write a valid heading with opening and closing tags
Build a simple outline: one H1, then H2 sections
Avoid the most common heading mistakes

content.md: An **`<h1>`** is a page's single most important heading. Browsers draw it large and bold, but its real job is *meaning*: it tells browsers, search engines, and screen readers what the entire page is about.

A heading introduces a section of content — like a newspaper headline or a chapter title. HTML gives you six levels: `<h1>` is the most important, down to `<h6>` for the smallest sub-heading. The H1 sits at the top of that outline. Everything else nests beneath it.
You choose a heading level for what it *means*, not for how big it looks. Size is the job of CSS. If you only need bigger text, use `font-size` — not a heading tag.

Before headings, an early web page was a flat wall of text. There was no machine-readable way to tell a title from a paragraph. Heading tags `<h1>`–`<h6>` were in HTML from its first public description in 1991, specifically to give documents **structure**.

content.caption: Headings form a document outline — a built-in table of contents that machines can read.

content.md:
**Remember**

- One main `<h1>` per page.
- Do not skip levels: `h1` → `h2` → `h3`.
- Write the H1 for humans, not as a keyword dump.

**Common mistakes**

- Several `<h1>` tags because they “look like titles”.
- Using a heading only to make text bigger.
- Skipping from `<h1>` to `<h3>`.
- Wrapping a logo in `<h1>` on every page.

children.md: In March 1989 at **CERN**, Tim Berners-Lee wrote *Information Management: A Proposal*. His manager Mike Sendall annotated it **“Vague but exciting.”** That note launched the work that became the World Wide Web.

CERN already used **SGML**, a markup system for technical papers. HTML borrowed heading levels from that world: one title, then sections, then sub-sections. The web made that structure something a *browser* could understand.

children.md: Browsers give `<h1>` a large default size and bold weight. That is only a default stylesheet. You can restyle headings with CSS without changing what they *mean*.

HTML5 described an “outline algorithm” that allowed more than one H1 inside sectioning elements. Browsers and screen readers never fully implemented it. In practice, **one H1 per page** is still the safest, clearest choice.

**Search (SEO).** Crawlers use headings to understand topic and structure. The H1 usually names the page. Headings are not a magic ranking lever — content quality matters more — but a clear outline helps engines summarize the page.
**Accessibility.** Screen readers such as VoiceOver, NVDA, and JAWS let a user open a *list of headings* and jump to a section. A correct `h1` → `h2` → `h3` tree is a map of the page.
**WCAG.** Relevant criteria include *1.3.1 Info and Relationships* and *2.4.6 Headings and Labels*. Skipping levels or using a heading only for style breaks that map, even when the page looks fine.

items.q: How many H1 elements should a page have?
items.a: By convention, one — the page’s main topic. HTML5 allowed more via the outline algorithm, but that algorithm was never fully implemented. One H1 remains the safest choice for SEO and accessibility.

items.q: What is the difference between <h1> and <title>?
items.a: <title> lives in <head> and labels the browser tab and search result. <h1> is the visible heading on the page. They often say similar things but serve different surfaces.
They help search engines understand structure and topic. They are not a strong standalone ranking factor. The bigger, more certain payoff is accessibility and readability.

items.q: What breaks if you skip from h1 to h3?
items.a: Visually, often nothing. A screen-reader user navigating by headings hits a gap and cannot tell whether a section is missing. That is an accessibility defect.

items.q: Why not just use CSS font-size?
items.a: Big text is not a heading. Heading tags carry meaning that CSS size does not. Search engines and assistive tech read the tag, not the pixels.

quickRecap: An **H1** names the whole page — it is the top of the heading outline.
It is used on every web page that has a main topic: articles, docs, product pages.
It exists so machines (browsers, search, screen readers) can read structure, not just style.
Use **one** H1, then H2 / H3 in order. Do not skip levels.
Do not use a heading only to make text bigger — that is CSS.
